report:
**Conclusion: generally no.** Regular vitamin C supplementation does **not** meaningfully prevent common colds for most people.

The strongest evidence is a Cochrane systematic review of placebo-controlled trials (≥200 mg/day). Across 29 comparisons involving 11,306 people in the general population, regular vitamin C did not reduce cold incidence. Thus, routine use specifically to avoid catching colds is not supported.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4/full

There is an important exception: in a small, distinct group exposed to brief periods of severe physical and/or cold stress—such as marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers on subarctic exercises—vitamin C approximately halved cold risk. This finding does not establish prevention benefit for typical daily life.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold

Vitamin C may instead have a modest effect *after* people get colds: the Cochrane review found regular supplementation modestly and consistently shortened symptom duration. But starting it only once symptoms begin has not shown a consistent benefit.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/

This agrees with Mayo Clinic’s summary that oral vitamin C supplements do not prevent the common cold.  
https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-vitamin-c/art-20363932
